title: Mucosal RNA Signatures in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: From Molecular Profiling to Clinical Prediction
content: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), exhibits substantial heterogeneity in clinical manifestations, disease course, and therapeutic response. Mucosal transcriptomic profiling has emerged as a promising approach to characterize this heterogeneity and identify molecular signatures with potential diagnostic, prognostic, and treatment-predictive applications. This narrative review critically examines evidence from microarray, bulk RNA-sequencing, and emerging single-cell and spatial transcriptomic studies, focusing on disease classification, inflammatory activity, relapse and progression, and response to biological therapies. Available findings implicate inflammatory signaling, epithelial dysfunction, stromal remodeling, and cell-specific immune programs, with several pretreatment signatures showing associations with therapeutic outcomes. However, molecular associations do not necessarily translate into reliable clinical prediction, and biomarkers reflecting disease severity may lack treatment-specific predictive value. Substantial heterogeneity in patient populations, intestinal sampling, analytical platforms, and outcome definitions, together with limited independent validation, complicates comparisons across studies. Although high-resolution transcriptomic technologies provide increasingly detailed insights into disease mechanisms, their added value for clinical decision-making remains uncertain. Future progress will require standardized methodologies, prospective multicenter validation, and demonstration that RNA-based biomarkers improve prediction beyond established clinical assessments. Ultimately, clinical translation will depend on developing reproducible, feasible assays that improve individualized IBD management.
